name: Rafael Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at my uncle Frank's garage in a market town, Bauer and Sons, though it's really just Frank, his old friend Walter and me. We do services, clutches, welding on old vans and a lot of farmers' pickups. Frank still writes the jobs on a chalkboard and I like it that way. I'm not the fastest, and Walter still has to check my torque settings, but I'm getting there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about life outside the garage?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Clara, she's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and we're getting married next June at our church. We rent a little cottage at the end of the high street. After paying the wedding deposits we've got about two months of costs left in savings. I've got a basic phone, I've never used one of these AI things and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, people get carried away with gadgets. At the garage we'd have a laugh about it, Walter would say he told us so. At church I'd say good, let people keep doing honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a relief, honestly. Frank's garage is steady, the farmers always need their pickups fixed, and family looks after family. If the computers stay as they are, I'll be welding farmers' vans in my uncle's garage until I'm grey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep learning from Walter, and keep saving for the wedding and after. Clara and I would put away about a hundred and fifty a month. Maybe I'd do the welding certificate at the college, because Frank says it's worth having.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how I like life, steady and familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the wedding costs, the hall alone was more than I earn in a month. But both families are chipping in. We'll manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if your uncle retired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's always said the garage comes to family, and that means me in time. I'd need to get much better first, and Walter would have to stay on a few years.

say: I'd say people got **carried away** with gadgets and I'm not surprised.
I'd tell people at church to keep doing **honest work**.
think: My uncle's **family garage** is steady, and farmers always need their pickups fixed.
I could **weld vans** there until I'm grey.
do: Save about **a hundred and fifty** a month with Clara.
Take the **welding certificate** at the college, as Frank suggests.
S0.quote: If the computers stay as they are, I'll be welding farmers' vans in my uncle's garage until I'm grey.
fieldNote: He leans on **family** as his security, and his uncle plans to pass on the garage.
**Wedding costs** are his only real pressure, shared by both families.
He's open about still needing **supervision** on torque settings.

steps.text: Keep learning from Walter at Bauer and Sons
Save a hundred and fifty a month with Clara
Take the welding certificate at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep their heads and work hard, there's always work for those who want it. I'd say it to Frank and Walter and to the men at church. I wouldn't go online, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the garage is fine for a while, because people still need hands under the bonnet. But Frank does the books and orders on paper, and if the suppliers move it all to AI, I'd have to learn. I never wanted to learn a computer, but I'd hate to be the reason my uncle's garage falls behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Clara to show me the basics on her laptop, slowly. I'd keep saving and maybe cut back on the wedding a little, fewer guests. I'd learn more from Walter, so the garage still has two good pairs of hands when he goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't like change I can't see the end of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cut the wedding. What would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the band, and a few of the second cousins. Clara's mum would be upset. But we'd rather start married without debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if things got hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the church. That's how my parents did it, and their parents. I don't expect the government to look after me.

say: I'd tell people to **work hard** because there's always work for the willing.
I'd say it to Frank, Walter and **the men at church**, not online.
think: The garage is fine for a while because cars still need **hands under the bonnet**.
If suppliers move to AI, I'd have to **learn computers** for Frank's sake.
do: Ask Clara to teach **laptop basics** slowly.
Cut back the **wedding guest list** to avoid debt.
Learn more from Walter so the garage keeps **two good mechanics**.
feel: Feels **uneasy** about change with **no clear end**.
S1.quote: I never wanted to learn a computer, but I'd hate to be the reason my uncle's garage falls behind.
fieldNote: He'd learn computers out of **family loyalty**, not curiosity.
He rejects **government help**, trusting family and church.
Cutting the **wedding** shows quiet caution despite a calm tone.

steps.text: Ask Clara to teach him laptop basics
Cut the band and some guests from the wedding
Take on more of Walter's hard jobs to learn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and the companies behind it should answer for it. I'd tell people at church to stick together and help each other. I wouldn't trust the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2031 a robot could do my uncle's work and mine. The farmers might buy their own machines. My uncle built a garage to hand down to family, and in five years there might be nothing left to hand down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as possible and save everything, maybe postpone the wedding a year. I'd talk to Frank about what the garage could become. I'd lean on family if things got hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's hard to sleep picturing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you postpone the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to marry Clara, but I'd want a small, cheap wedding. We'd keep the church and drop the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That hard work still matters, even if machines do the work. And that family is what lasts.

say: I'd say the **companies behind it** should answer for it.
I'd urge people at church to **stick together** rather than trust government.
think: By 2031 a robot could do **my uncle's work** and mine.
There might be **nothing left** of the family garage to hand down.
do: Shrink the wedding to **church only**, dropping the hall.
Talk to Frank about the **garage's future** and lean on family.
S2.quote: My uncle built a garage to hand down to family, and in five years there might be nothing left to hand down.
fieldNote: His grief is for the **family inheritance** more than his own job.
He still distrusts **government**, relying on family and church.
He'd shrink the **wedding** but not delay marrying.

steps.text: Save everything possible from every week's pay
Hold a small church wedding without the hall
Ask his family for help if work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to prepare, so families and churches should start helping each other now. I'd talk about apprenticeships and keeping skills alive. I'd still not trust the government much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, eight years of hands-on work is better than five, but it's still not long. I'd be thirty-five when the robots come. Five years warning means I'd still be married and maybe a father before the robots take my hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the welding certificate and learn the business side with Frank. I'd keep saving and maybe look at buying into the garage with family money. I'd stay put in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a bit more room to breathe than with two years. I'd still be praying about it most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy into the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if robots come, I'd rather own them than work for them. Frank would help, and my dad might put money in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn enough to keep the books, if Clara helped. I wouldn't enjoy it.

I'd talk about **apprenticeships** and keeping skills alive.
think: I'd have **eight years** of hands-on work before robots arrive.
I'd be **thirty-five**, married and maybe a father.
do: Get the **welding certificate** and learn the business side.
Consider **buying into the garage** with family money.
S3.quote: Five years warning means I'd still be married and maybe a father before the robots take my hands-on work.
fieldNote: He'd rather **own the robots** than work for them.
He'd use **family money** to buy into the garage.
He'd learn just enough AI for the **books**.

steps.text: Get the welding certificate at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people work hard and plan. I'd tell the young people at church to learn a trade anyway. I'd keep trusting family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd be forty when the robots come, probably running the garage. With ten years warning, I'd have time to take over my uncle's garage and decide what it becomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the business and get the certificates, marry Clara as planned, and save steadily. I'd look at buying a robot for the garage when they arrive. I'd keep family close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, if I'm honest, because forty is no age to start again. But steady, because there's time to sort it with family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a couple of years after the wedding. Clara wants kids, so do I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell them about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, learn how to own something, and always help family. That's what my dad told me, and it's still true.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** for people who work hard and plan.
I'd tell young people at church to **learn a trade** anyway.
think: I'd be **forty** when robots arrive, probably running the garage.
I'd have time to **take over** my uncle's garage.
do: Marry Clara **as planned** and save steadily.
Look at **buying a robot** for the garage when they arrive.
S4.quote: With ten years warning, I'd have time to take over my uncle's garage and decide what it becomes.
fieldNote: He plans to **own** the future rather than fight it.
Family plans stay **on track** with a decade's warning.
He'd buy a **robot** rather than be replaced by one.

steps.text: Learn the garage's business side from Frank
Marry Clara as planned and have children
Buy a workshop robot for the garage when available

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit before the wedding and before Frank can hand on the garage. What would help is family and community sticking together, and apprenticeships that keep people working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith and family. People forget that when work disappears, it's family and church that catch you, not a screen.

headlineQuote: People forget that when work disappears, it's family and church that catch you, not a screen.
portrait: Rafael works at his **uncle's garage**, learning from an older mechanic.
He's **engaged to Clara** and planning a church wedding next June.
He **avoids AI** and trusts family and church over government.
He'd learn computers out of **loyalty** to the family business.
With time, he plans to **own the garage** and possibly its robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, before his wedding and before inheriting the garage.
whatWouldHelp: **Family and community** support, and **apprenticeships** that keep people working.
